title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities
claim: Linear representations suffice for linear recovery, but axis-aligned recovery needs non-negativity plus the right data structure.
layout: 4 line plots in 2x2 grid, plus 5x2 heatmap column at right
description: The figure has five panels. Panels A–D form a 2x2 grid of training curves, with training step on a log x-axis from 10^3 to 10^6. The top row (A, B) plots population disentanglement and the bottom row (C, D) plots individual (axis-aligned) disentanglement. The left column uses the Hypersphere DGP and the middle column uses the Sparse DGP. Each plot has a blue line for linear representation and an orange line for non-negative representation, with shaded error bands. In A and B both curves reach about 1.0 (A's orange curve plateaus slightly below). In C the orange curve falls to about 0.4 while blue stays near 0.77. In D the orange curve rises to about 0.9 and crosses above the blue one. Panel E, on the right, shows five rows of 5x5 matrix heatmaps. The Linear column is a diffuse blue/red mixture and the ReLU column is sparse, permutation-like red entries. The eye goes first to the crossing curves in D.
caption: Linear and axis-aligned latent recovery at exact capacity. A) Hyperspherical DGP [ref], training a neural network with linear representation (i.e., no final activation function, blue) and a non-negative representation (ReLU, orange); Disentanglement between true latent variables (\(z\)) and learned neural representations (\(\hat{z}=h(z)\)), measured up to arbitrary linear transformations (\(W\)). B) Our proposed sparse, non-negative DGP, same architectures as on the left (with/without activation function), linear disentanglement reported. C) Same as A, but disentanglement is measured only up to permutations (\(P\)), measuring axis-aligned latent variable recovery. D) Same as B but individual, axis-aligned disentanglement measured. E) Sample visualizations of five optimization runs, learned linear representation \(h(z)=Az\) showing a clear permutation only for the non-negative case. Shaded areas in all plots indicate standard error of the mean over 10 random seeds.
abstract: Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.
